prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength opened a new regime of precision at the 10^-18 level in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B004) as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye, and I want to state the scientific argument rather than lean on the count, as the chair asked. The new idea is the magic-wavelength lattice: a trap wavelength at which the dynamic polarizabilities of the two clock states are equal, so the trapping light shifts the clock transition by nothing to first order while thousands of neutral atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no Doppler or recoil shift. That is a statement about atomic structure and about how to control every perturbation, and it is why the uncertainty reached the 1e-18 level, roughly two orders better than caesium. Katori proposed it and realised the first strontium lattice clock. Ye took it to the accuracy frontier, with the record systematic budgets and the many-body Fermi-degenerate clock, where the lattice becomes a controlled many-body system and not only a ruler. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) agree at that level and intercontinental comparisons confirm it, which is the robustness I look for as someone who sits next to experimental teams. On the chair's question, I answer that the 2005 prize honoured the comb as a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions; neither contains trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, so the lattice clock is a separable invention with a separate step in accuracy. The citation must name the lattice and the magic wavelength, as Danielsson, Lindroth and Mehlig asked. On timing, I do not think the committee needs to wait for the redefinition of the second: the award rests on demonstrated and reproduced performance, and a redefinition would only confirm it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains continuity with the 2005 and 2012 prizes: a sceptic can read the lattice clock as the next refinement of precision spectroscopy and a measurement tool, not a surprise in nature, and Danielsson is right that the constants tests so far give null results, so I would justify the prize by the new capability and the resolved physics (millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body clock physics) and not by a discovery about constants. Credit is the second weakness: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow and Oates made early or record contributions that a two-name prize leaves out, and I cannot show a single decisive contribution that would justify a third name over the proposal (Katori) and the sustained frontier (Ye). The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the payoff is prospective.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether I see any scientific obstacle to B004, as opposed to simply preferring my own field, given that it was third on my opening ballot.
responses.response: I see none. My opening first choice was circuit QED because it is my field, and I now treat that as a bias to discount. The scientific obstacles I could find are the ones the committee already lists: overlap wording, the Lemonde and SYRTE credit, and the pending redefinition. None of these affects whether the physics is original or reproduced. I also accept your point that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes a second circuit award this soon hard to defend, so I no longer treat B034 as a serious alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson asks that the citation name the lattice concept explicitly to separate it from 2005 and 2012, and says the constants tests so far give null results, so the prize should be justified by capability.
responses.response: I agree on both. The proposed citation names the magic-wavelength lattice itself. On the foundations, I would not claim a discovery about constants; I would say the clock now resolves relativistic redshift across millimetres and constrains variation and dark-matter couplings, which is a new regime of measurement that tests nature even when the answer so far is null. In round 1 I leaned on that more than you did. I now rest the case on capability plus the new many-body and redshift physics.

responses.point: Eriksson says that if atomic-physics colleagues judge the clock sufficiently distinct from 2005 and 2012 he would not stand in the way, and asks that B010 be considered in a following year.
responses.response: I take that as the question for the AMO side and answer it directly: the lattice clock is distinct, because the new element is the magic-wavelength condition on atomic polarizabilities and the control of the residual lattice-induced shifts, not the comb and not ion control. I agree B010 is the strongest condensed-matter case on the list and that the missing pairing mechanism need not block a prize worded around flat bands and correlated phases. The obstacles for this year are Yuan Cao and the early moire theorists outside the trio, and device variability, and I would favour revisiting B010 when those are better settled.

responses.point: Olsson wants the historical record checked on whether Katori's proposal or the first operational clock marks the original contribution, and asks for a case that circuit QED is distinct from macroscopic quantum tunnelling.
responses.response: On B004, I would record explicitly that the credit is Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's sustained leadership of accuracy and the many-body clock; that is a deliberate choice and not an assumption, and the Lemonde group's near-simultaneous work should be acknowledged in the committee text, not in the prize. On B034, I will not make the case for distinctness. The distinction exists, since circuit QED is single-photon strong coupling and not tunnelling, but I agree with you that the Blais and Girvin boundary is unresolved among people who know the field, and I have the conflict, so I step back.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with a quantum-technology topic such as circuit QED is worth the loss of credit coherence.
responses.response: I do not propose a second part. A circuit-QED part would be advocated by the member with the closest tie to the field and would need a three-from-four cut that two members already draw differently, so credit coherence would suffer. I also agree with Pearce that atom interferometry (B036) is too close in laser-cooling heritage to pair with clocks in the same year. The coherence of a single topic with two names is a real advantage.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, after hearing the lattice-clock case, accepts it as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the final citation wording makes the magic-wavelength lattice the subject.
Whether two names fairly capture the record given Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates and the SYRTE group; I could not find a specific decisive contribution that would justify a third name.
Whether the redefinition of the second should come first; I think performance already justifies the award but the redefinition would strengthen it.
Whether B010 will be mature enough in a later year once the pairing mechanism and the Yuan Cao attribution question are clearer.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work on superconducting circuits at Chalmers, so I have a possible conflict on B034 (circuit QED) and B043 (mechanical oscillators); I do not advocate either, have dropped B034 from my alternatives, and would recuse on them if the committee requires. Olsson is a Chalmers colleague and Kroll sits on the WACQT management team; I do not regard this as a recusal matter for B004. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye and no conflict on B004 or on my alternatives B010 and B036 is apparent from my profile.
